chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Ibn Mahbub from Ali ibn Ri'ab from Abu Ubaydah from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) in

A woman drank medicine while pregnant to miscarry her child, and she gave birth. He said: If it had bone with flesh grown upon it, and its hearing and sight were opened, then upon her is a diyah (blood money) which she pays to its father. He said: And if it was a fetus, a 'alaqah (clot) or a mudghah (chewed flesh), then upon her is forty dinars or a ghurrat (fixed payment) which she pays to its father. I said: So she does not inherit from her child from its diyah? He said: No, because she killed it. And this interpretation does not contradict the narration of Al-Halabi and Abu Ubaydah that the woman was in labor, because it is not impossible that she was in labor even if the child was not complete, being a miscarriage. So there is no objection to that in any case. And it is possible that these narrations be carried upon a type of taqiyyah (dissimulation), because that is the view of many of the Sunnis, and it has been narrated from the Prophet (peace be upon him and his pure family).

key_terms.أَبُوهِ: Its father (referring to the father of the fetus)
key_terms.تَقِيَّة: Dissimulation or precautionary concealment of belief
key_terms.دِيَة: Blood money or financial compensation for homicide or injury
key_terms.عَلَقَة: A stage of fetal development, literally a 'clot'
key_terms.غُرَّة: A fixed payment of blood money, typically for specific injuries or fetal loss
key_terms.مُضْغَة: A stage of fetal development, literally a 'chewed piece'

ai.seo_question: What is the diyah for a miscarried fetus according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Isfahar establishes the legal framework for abortion, distinguishing between early-stage fetuses (alaqah or mudghah) and those with developed senses, assigning a fixed fine (ghurrat) versus blood money (diyah). It clarifies that the mother inherits no compensation as she is the direct cause of death, while reconciling apparent contradictions in narrations through the principle of taqiyyah, reflecting the juristic caution of the Shia school regarding fetal status.
